profiles.label: Volkswagen GTI (Mk6, 2010–2014)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the Mk6 GTI is the cheap, genuinely good daily driver: a torquey 200hp EA888 2.0T, a crisp 6-speed manual, a hatch that swallows Costco runs and a bike with the seats down, and a chassis that is happy on Highway 1 and Laureles Grade. It is not an appreciating asset and never will be, so every dollar should go toward buying a documented, stock, un-tuned car rather than chasing a rare spec. The entire risk in this generation is engine-adjacent maintenance debt — timing chain tensioner, cam follower, PCV, water pump, carbon — that a neglected car hides and a fastidious owner documents. A $11–14k car with a thick folder is worth far more than a $9k car with a clean CarFax and no receipts.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing chain tensioner (EA888 Gen1/Gen2, CCTA/CBFA): the defining failure of this engine family. The early hydraulic tensioner can lose tension on a cold start or after a hot shutdown, the chain skips teeth, and the engine bends valves — a $4,000–7,000 event. VW released revised tensioners (the 'K' / 06K109467K-series updates); 2012 cars may or may not have had it done. Symptoms: rattle for 1–3 seconds on cold start, a P0016/P0017 crank-cam correlation code. Demand a receipt for tensioner replacement or budget $900–1,600 to do it preemptively. This is the single most important piece of paper on the car. 2) High-pressure fuel pump cam follower: a small hardened bucket riding a cam lobe, meant to be inspected every 30–40k miles. When it wears through, metal enters the HPFP and the cam lobe is destroyed — $1,500–3,000. The part itself is ~$25. Look for a receipt or pull it during PPI. 3) PCV / oil separator valve (the black plastic assembly on the valve cover): diaphragm tears at 60–100k. Symptoms are rough idle, a whistle or suction noise, high crankcase vacuum that pulls the rear main seal out and causes an oil leak, and misfire codes. $350–550 installed; if it has already blown the rear main seal, add $1,000–1,500 for transmission-out seal work. 4) Plastic water pump / thermostat housing: leaks at 70–110k, often first visible as pink crust at the front of the block or a low-coolant light. $700–1,000 installed since the pump is timing-chain-driven and the job is involved. 5) Carbon buildup on intake valves: direct injection with no port wash. By 70–90k expect rough cold idle, misfires under load, and a soft midrange. Walnut blasting runs $450–800 and should recur every 60–80k. Ask when it was last done. 6) Intake manifold runner flap motor: P2015 code, check engine light, occasionally limp mode. The flap position sensor fails; a full manifold is $450–700 installed, bracket-repair kits are cheaper but a bandage. 7) Diverter valve (turbo bypass): the early diaphragm-style DV tears; revised piston-style unit (06H145710D) is a $150–250 fix. Symptoms are a flutter/whoosh, soft boost, P0299 underboost. Many have already been done. 8) DSG (DQ250 wet-clutch) if so equipped: mandatory fluid and filter service every 40k at $400–650; mechatronic unit failure is $2,500–3,800 and clutch packs are $1,800–2,500. Symptoms are shudder from a stop, hesitation in first-to-second, flare on shifts. This buyer should strongly prefer the 6-speed manual, which avoids the whole category. 9) Manual clutch and dual-mass flywheel: typically 90–130k on a non-abused car, more like 50k on a tuned one. $1,600–2,400 installed. Chatter at takeoff, rattle at idle in neutral that quiets with the pedal down, and a high engagement point are the tells. 10) Turbo K03 wastegate actuator rod: develops play and rattles at low RPM under light load; also causes boost control faults. Rebuilt/replacement turbo is $1,300–2,000; some cars only need an actuator. 11) Suspension bushings and mounts: front lower control arm bushings, sway bar end links, and rear shock mounts are all soft by 90k. Clunking over expansion joints, wandering, uneven tire wear. $700–1,400 to refresh front end properly. 12) Electrical nuisances that are near-universal: door lock actuator/microswitch failures ($250–400 per door), rear hatch handle microswitch (hatch won't open from the outside), window regulator clips, and on Autobahn cars the Xenon/AFS headlight module or ballast ($400–900). 13) Water intrusion: sunroof drains clog and wet the headliner or the driver's footwell; a soaked floor can kill the comfort control module under the seat. Lift the carpet corners and smell for mildew. 14) Oil consumption: some Gen1/Gen2 EA888s use a quart per 1,000–1,500 miles through ring/PCV issues. Ask the seller directly and check the dipstick against reported last-change mileage. 15) Tuning and modification: Stage 1/Stage 2 software plus an aggressive clutch, aftermarket diverter, or a big intake stresses t
profiles.immediate_repairs: Oil and filter with 502.00-spec synthetic; inspect (and almost certainly replace) the HPFP cam follower; full scan for stored/pending codes and ECU flash count; replace ignition coils and plugs if unknown ($250–450); replace the diverter valve if it is still the original diaphragm unit; fix any PCV whistle or rough idle; front and rear brakes if pads/rotors are marginal ($500–800); four matched tires if mismatched ($700–1,000); DSG fluid + filter immediately if automatic and no record; new wipers, cabin filter, and a battery if it is more than five years old.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Timing chain tensioner update if there is no receipt ($900–1,600); walnut-blast intake valve carbon cleaning ($450–800); water pump and thermostat housing if any seepage ($700–1,000); PCV assembly ($350–550); front control arm bushings and sway bar end links ($700–1,200); intake manifold if P2015 appears ($450–700); rear main seal if a PCV failure preceded purchase; clutch and DMF if the car is past 100k or the engagement point is high; a serpentine belt, coolant flush, and brake fluid flush as general catch-up.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission is worth a clear premium over DSG to enthusiast buyers and lowers long-term risk; DSG cars with no fluid-service history should be discounted hard. Four-door bodies sell for slightly more than two-doors to practical buyers, though enthusiasts often prefer the two-door; Autobahn (leather, sunroof, Xenons, Dynaudio) and 2013–14 Wolfsburg Edition trims add modest money. Unmodified, one- or two-owner California cars with the plaid cloth interior and documented tensioner/cam-follower/carbon work sit at the top of the range — roughly $10–15k for clean 70–110k-mile examples — while tuned, high-mile, or no-records cars fall to $6–9k and are not actually cheaper once you fund the deferred work. Color matters little except that Tornado Red, Candy White, and Carbon Steel Gray move faster than silver.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2012 with 90–120k miles is due for a cluster of age items at once: tensioner update if not done, carbon cleaning, PCV, water pump/thermostat housing, coolant and brake fluid flushes, and a front-end bushing refresh — realistically $2,500–4,000 spread over the first year. Rubber items (motor mounts, hoses, hatch struts, door seals) are 13+ years old regardless of mileage, and a California car will be rust-free but sun-baked, so expect a cracked dash trim, faded headlight lenses, and a tired battery.

profiles.label: Volvo Amazon 122S Wagon (P220)
profiles.framing: This is a charming, genuinely usable 1960s wagon that the buyer will drive on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not a trailer queen. Mechanically it is simple, over-built, and fully supported by the aftermarket (VP Autoparts, Skandix, IPD), so the real questions are rust, brakes, front-end wear, and whether the car has been honestly sorted or merely made pretty. On a 4-speed non-overdrive car with a 4.10-ish final drive, 65-70 mph is a buzzy 3,400-3,700 rpm — acceptable for local use, tiring for long freeway hauls, and the single biggest driveability limit worth pricing in. Documentation matters more than shine: a repainted car with a bypassed heater, dead horn, and dead parking brake is telling you where the money went.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Structural rust is the only true value-killer. Check the front frame rails/torque boxes ahead of the firewall, the jacking points and rocker/sill closing panels, the floor pans under both front seats, the battery tray area, and — wagon-specific — the rear cargo floor, the spare-tire well, the rear spring hangers/shackle mounts, and the D-pillar/rear arch seams. A repaint in 2021 with 'spots of overspray' means the underside and seams must be photographed, not assumed. Cut-and-weld floor/rocker repair runs $1,500-$5,000+; frame-rail or spring-hanger repair can exceed the car's value. 2) Wagon tailgate rust: the lower gate's inner skin and bottom seam and the upper gate's glass frame trap water; hinges sag and the upper latch wears (rebuilt latches are available ~$150-300). A rusted lower gate is a hard-to-source, expensive panel. 3) King-pin front suspension (not ball joints): pins and bushings need grease every ~1,500 miles and are almost always neglected. Symptoms: clunk over bumps, wander, uneven front tire wear, vertical play when levered at the wheel. Proper rebuild with reaming/line-boring of the new bushings is $800-1,800 for the pair; shops that just press bushings in produce a car that binds. 4) Steering box (Bishop cam / cam-and-roller) develops 2-4 inches of play at the rim; also idler arm, tie rod ends, and the drag link. Rebuild box $500-900 exchanged, plus $300-600 in links. 5) Brakes: front Girling discs with rear drums; 1967 cars use a dual-circuit master. Expect seized caliper pistons, weeping wheel cylinders, and 30-year-old flex hoses. The parking brake acting on the rear drums seizes at the cables and levers constantly — 'parking brake doesn't work' is normal, and it is both a safety and a California-registration/inspection annoyance. Full system refresh (master, calipers, wheel cylinders, hoses, shoes, pads, cables) is $1,200-2,200. 6) B18B engine (dual SU HS6 carbs, ~95 hp): the five-main bottom end is famously durable, but the camshaft drive gear is a fiber/composite gear that strips teeth without warning, typically past 80-100k miles or after decades of age — a $60 part that requires the timing cover off ($400-800 labor); an aluminum-hub steel/fiber replacement receipt is exactly what you want to see. 7) Oil leaks: rear main and front crank seal weep, and a clogged 'flame trap' (PCV oil trap) in the intake pressurizes the crankcase and pushes oil past every seal. Cleaning/replacing the flame trap and hose is a $40 fix that prevents a $1,200 diagnosis. 8) Twin SU carbs go out of sync as throttle shafts and jet seals wear: hard cold starts, uneven idle, plug fouling, 16-18 mpg where 24-26 is normal. Rebuild/rebush the pair $500-900; many cars have been 'fixed' with a single Weber downdraft conversion, which runs but is a de-originalizing move. 9) Cooling: original radiators are usually clogged or already recored; water pump, thermostat housing corrosion, and hardened hoses are routine. Recore $400-650. Watch for overheating in traffic — a sorted Amazon should not. 10) Heater system: the box, valve, and core are buried behind the dash and the valve seizes; 'heater bypassed' is a common shortcut. Restoring heat/defrost properly means core rebuild plus box removal, $800-1,800. No defroster is a real problem in Carmel fog. 11) Electrical: many 1967 cars still have a generator/regulator (alternator conversion $350-700), plus corroded fuse block and ground straps, failed horn ring contact, dead wiper motors, and brittle cloth-loom wiring at the headlight switch and column. A dead radio/horn usually signals an un-restored harness. 12) Drivetrain: M40 4-speed is stout but the clutch hydraulics (master/slave) and the clutch cross-shaft bushings wear; second-gear synchro is the first to go. The Spicer rear axle leaks at the pinion seal and the axle-tube/backing-plate seals contaminate rear shoes. Retrofitting an M41 with Laycock J-type overdrive is the single best driveability upgrade, $2,000-3,500 installed — an
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full brake safety pass: flex hoses, wheel cylinders, caliper rebuild/replacement, fluid flush, and parking brake cables/levers freed and adjusted ($900-1,800). Replace all rubber fuel lines and inspect the tank/pump ($250-500). Flame trap/PCV service and full fluid change including gearbox and rear axle ($200-350). Twin SU sync, points/condenser/cap/rotor, valve adjustment, timing ($400-800). Front-end inspection with king-pin grease service and tie-rod/idler tightening; expect a king-pin rebuild if there is measurable play ($800-1,800). Re-commission the horn and wipers (safety/registration) and diagnose the bypassed heater ($300-900). Fresh date-coded tires if the current set is over six years old ($700-1,000). Seat-belt condition and mounting check.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Camshaft fiber-gear replacement if there is no receipt ($500-900 installed). Radiator recore and cooling-system refresh including water pump and hoses ($700-1,200). Heater core/valve restoration for real defrost ($800-1,800). Alternator conversion and fuse-block/ground-strap refresh ($500-1,000). Steering box rebuild or exchange plus idler arm ($700-1,400). Rear main/front seal and pinion-seal attention if oil consumption or drips persist ($600-1,500). Weatherstrip and tailgate seal replacement to stop cargo-floor water intrusion ($800-1,800). Seat cushion and headliner repair ($800-2,000). Strongly consider an M41 overdrive gearbox swap for freeway usability ($2,000-3,500). Localized rust repair on rockers/jack points/spare well if the PPI finds early scale ($1,500-4,000).
profiles.market_notes: Wagons (P220) command a clear premium over 122S sedans and two-doors; a 4-speed is essential, an original overdrive (M41) car adds roughly $2,000-4,000, and the rare BW35 automatic subtracts heavily. Documented rust-free dry-state provenance, photographed underside, and a receipt file move price more than paint gloss — driver-quality repainted cars with deferred mechanicals cluster around $9,000-16,000, genuinely sorted examples with overdrive, working heat, and a brake/front-end file reach $20,000-30,000, and true restorations go higher. Period colors with the split tailgate, correct 15-inch steels with hubcaps, and honest unmolested engine bays (twin SUs, not a Weber) support the top of the band; East Coast/Southeast cars carry a rust discount plus $1,200-1,800 shipping to the Monterey Peninsula. Non-functioning heater, parking brake, and horn are cheap-sounding items that reliably knock $1,500-3,000 off bidder confidence because they signal an unfinished car.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a ~58-year-old car needs a full safety re-commission regardless of cosmetics: all brake hydraulics and flex hoses, all rubber fuel lines, cooling system, weatherstrip, and date-expired tires. Budget $3,500-6,000 in the first year just to bring deferred rubber, brakes, and front-end wear current, plus $2,000-3,500 more if you want overdrive and working heat/defrost for real Monterey Peninsula use.

profiles.label: Volvo S60 (P3, 2011–2018; 2014+ facelift)
profiles.framing: This is a fast, comfortable, very safe all-weather sedan with an unusual drivetrain — Volvo's transverse 3.0L turbocharged inline-six (B6304T4) with Haldex AWD and an Aisin six-speed automatic — wrapped in one of the better-looking interiors of the era. For a Carmel-based driver it makes sense as a quiet Highway 1 commuter and weekend road-trip car, not as an appreciating asset: P3 S60s depreciate hard and are worth roughly parts-and-labor money, so the entire purchase decision hinges on documented maintenance rather than badge or color. The T6 R-Design Platinum is the desirable spec (325 hp, sport chassis, Nappa/contour seats, Harman Kardon, nav, BLIS), and the dealer-installed Polestar Performance Optimization is a factory-sanctioned flash rather than an aftermarket tune — acceptable to a 'documented, unmodified' buyer if there is a Volvo dealer receipt for it. The core risk is that a neglected example can hand you a five-figure repair (timing chain at the flywheel end, transmission, angle gear) on a car worth five figures.
profiles.weak_points: PCV / oil trap system: the SI6 crankcase ventilation box clogs with oil coke, typically 80k–130k miles, driving crankcase pressure up until it blows out the rear main seal or front crank seal, pushes oil past turbo seals, and causes a whistling/moaning idle. The dipstick or glove test is the field diagnostic; proper replacement means intake manifold off and runs $900–$1,800. If the oil trap was never done and there is a rear main leak, budget for the seal too (transmission out, $1,500–$2,500). Timing chain and guides: unlike most cars, the SI6's chain lives at the flywheel end of the engine, so chain, guide, and tensioner service requires separating engine and transmission — $3,000–$5,000. Symptom is a brief rattle or diesel-like clatter on cold start; any such noise is a hard walk-away unless the job has a receipt. Angle gear (bevel gear/PTU): the splined collar between transmission and angle gear wears and strips, especially where fluid was never changed; symptoms are a whine under load, driveline slop, or metallic glitter on the drain plug. Replacement is $1,500–$3,000 with the collar upgrade; fluid should be changed every ~30k and is almost never done. Haldex Gen IV AWD: pump strainer/filter clogs and the pump burns out, leaving front-wheel drive and a 'AWD Service Required' message; filter+fluid is a $250–$400 service every 30–40k, pump replacement $700–$1,200. Aisin AW TF-80SC six-speed: Volvo called the fluid lifetime, and it isn't. Expect torque-converter shudder at light throttle 40–60 mph, flare or clunk on the 2–3 shift, and eventual valve body/solenoid faults after 100k. Fluid+filter service is $400–$600 if done in time; a rebuilt or used unit is $3,500–$5,500. Turbo and boost plumbing: the twin-scroll turbo's wastegate actuator, bypass (diverter) valve, and charge pipe couplings leak, causing a boost-drop code, lag, or a limp-mode 'Reduced Performance' message; actuator/valve work $400–$900, turbo $2,000+. Coolant and thermostat: expansion tanks crack at the seam, thermostat housings and the coolant pipe behind the engine weep; a hot-spot overheat on this alloy six is expensive, so pressure-test it. $300–$900 typical. Water intrusion and electronics: sunroof and cowl drains plug and soak the passenger and driver footwells, which is where the CEM sits; symptoms are damp carpet padding, random warning messages, battery drain, and door/seat module faults. Cost ranges from a $150 drain cleanout to a $1,200+ module and harness repair — check under the carpet with your hand, not your eyes. Electric parking brake: the rear caliper-integrated EPB actuators seize or the module throws faults, usually after a winter car sits; $500–$900 per side including caliper. Suspension and R-Design chassis: front lower control arm bushings and sway bar end links wear by 80k, strut mounts clunk, and the R-Design's 18/19-inch wheels with low-profile tires bend on potholes and make the ride harsh. Full front control arms, links, and an alignment run $1,200–$1,800. Ignition and fuel: six coils and plugs cause rough idle/misfire codes by 90k–110k ($500–$800 to do all six properly); high-pressure fuel pump and injector faults show as long crank or fuel trim codes. Miscellaneous age items: power steering pump/rack and hose seepage (this is still a hydraulic system), front engine torque rod (dogbone) bushing collapse causing a shudder on take-off ($200–$400), A/C evaporator temp sensor and condenser leaks, and the Sensus/RTI infotainment dying or the backup camera fogging. Rust is rare on a lifelong California car but check rear subframe and rear-wheel-arch seams on any Northeast/Midwest re-registration.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up on arrival: transmission fluid and filter, angle gear fluid, Haldex fluid and filter/strainer, engine oil with a correct-spec low-ash 0W-30/5W-30, brake fluid flush, and coolant if unknown. Crankcase pressure (PCV) test and oil trap replacement if pressure is high. Tires almost always need replacing on an R-Design — a matched set of 19s is $900–$1,400 — plus an alignment. Front brake pads/rotors if under-spec, cabin and engine air filters, wiper blades, and a battery load test (these cars are hard on batteries and a weak one causes phantom module faults). Clear the sunroof and cowl drains and pull back the carpet to confirm the footwells are dry.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Spark plugs and coil pack replacement if not documented, front lower control arm bushings/ball joints and sway bar links, front engine torque rod bushing, expansion tank and any weeping coolant hoses, turbo bypass/wastegate actuator if boost codes appear, rear main or front crank seal if the PCV was neglected before you bought it, EPB actuator on one rear corner, and one or two nuisance electrical items (door module, camera, headlight ballast/bulb on the active bi-xenons at $400–$700 per side).
profiles.market_notes: T6 AWD R-Design with the Platinum package sits at the top of the P3 S60 range and commands a meaningful premium over a T5 FWD, but the whole model line is deep in depreciation — condition and records move price far more than trim. Documented transmission, angle gear, Haldex, and PCV service is worth more to an informed buyer than 20k fewer miles; a no-records 90k car and a receipted 120k car should not trade at the same number. Distinctive R-Design colors (Rebel Blue, Passion Red) and a clean one- or two-owner California history help liquidity; Polestar Performance Optimization is a mild positive only when there's a Volvo dealer invoice for it, and any non-Polestar tune, exhaust, or lowering springs is a discount. Mileage bands matter: sub-70k cars ask a premium, 70k–110k is the value sweet spot if documented, and above 120k the car is priced against its next big repair.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a decade-old Swedish turbo six arrives with every 'lifetime' fluid still original: plan a one-time $1,500–$2,500 catch-up covering transmission, angle gear, Haldex, coolant, and brake fluid, plus the PCV oil trap if pressure is high. Rubber-and-plastic age items — expansion tank, coolant hoses, control arm bushings, torque rod, sunroof drains, and the battery — should be addressed proactively rather than after they strand the car. Tires and an alignment are near-certain on an R-Design regardless of tread depth, since matched date codes on 19s are rare on cheap examples.

profiles.label: Volvo V60 T8 Polestar Engineered (SPA, Recharge Twin Engine)
profiles.framing: This is the fastest, most focused version of Volvo's last real sport wagon: a 400–455 hp plug-in hybrid with Öhlins manually adjustable dampers, Brembo front brakes, a front strut brace and a genuinely useful 50/50 estate body. For a Carmel-based buyer it is a one-car answer — quiet EV commuting to Monterey, a 30-mile electric range for town errands, and a car that can cover Highway 1 or a Bay Area run at speed in comfort. Buy it as a depreciated, warranty-backed daily driver, not as an appreciating asset: the complexity is high, dealer dependence is real, and a 2019–2021 PE (supercharger + 11.6 kWh pack) is a meaningfully different, more fragile machine than a 2022–2024 (turbo-only, 18.8 kWh, 455 hp). What matters most is documented dealer service, current software, verified high-voltage battery health, remaining factory/hybrid warranty, and a rust-free underbody if the car came from a salt state.
profiles.weak_points: 1) High-voltage battery and hybrid control system: 11.6 kWh pack on 2019–21, 18.8 kWh on 2022+. Failures are usually module-level or BMS/contactor related and announce themselves as 'Hybrid system service required,' reduced EV range, or refusal to charge. Under the 8-year/100,000-mile hybrid warranty this is free; out of warranty, module or pack replacement runs roughly $6,000–15,000+ and is dealer-only. Insist on a VIDA-based battery state-of-health/capacity report, not the driver display's guess-o-meter. 2) HV battery and engine cooling circuits: multiple electric coolant pumps, a separate battery chiller/valve block, and a PTC cabin heater. Weeping pumps, low-coolant warnings and 'reduced hybrid performance' messages appear from 40k miles; pumps are $400–900 each installed, and neglected coolant accelerates pack degradation. 3) Onboard charger (OBC) and charge port: J1772 3.7 kW (2019–21) / 6.4 kW (2022+). OBC faults produce charging aborts and stored DTCs; replacement is $1,800–3,000. Test an actual full Level 2 charge cycle, not just a plug-in handshake. 4) 12V/support battery and parasitic drain: SPA cars are notorious for flat 12V batteries after sitting, which then throw a Christmas tree of bogus faults. Expect the AGM main and (on some builds) the small support battery to be consumables at 4–6 years, $300–600 for the pair, plus a drain test if the car has sat. 5) Supercharger (2019–2021 T8 only): the Roots blower's electromagnetic clutch and bearings whine, rattle at idle, or seize; a blower assembly is $2,500–4,000 installed. 2022+ cars deleted the supercharger — one of the best reasons to prefer the later spec. 6) Timing belt on the VEA B4204T engine: rubber belt, age-sensitive, with a nominal ~10 year/150k-mile interval. A 2019–2020 car is already inside the age window; budget $1,200–2,200 and get the receipt if claimed done. Also inspect the PCV/valve-cover diaphragm (whistling, rough idle, oil weep) and the crank pulley/decoupler. 7) Fuel dilution and short-trip wear: T8s driven mostly on electricity cook the oil with fuel because the engine rarely reaches temperature. Look for 7,500-mile/annual oil changes minimum (ideally every 5,000 on a town-driven car); ask for a used-oil analysis or at least check for fuel smell and overfull dipstick level. Carbon buildup on the direct-injection intake valves shows up as cold-start stumble and misfires by 60–90k miles; walnut blasting is $700–1,200. 8) Aisin 8-speed transaxle with integrated crank-mounted starter/generator (CISG): Volvo calls the fluid lifetime; it is not. Harsh 1-2 shifts, hesitation off the line, or clunks during engine start/stop blending are warning signs. Fluid and filter service is $400–700; a transaxle or CISG failure is $6,000–9,000. 9) Electric rear axle drive (ERAD) unit: the rear wheels are motor-driven with no driveshaft. Listen for whine under EV acceleration and a growl on coast; check the reduction-gear housing for weeping oil. Replacement is a $4,000–6,000 dealer job. 10) Öhlins DFV dampers: manually adjustable, no electronic control. They leak at the shaft seals, and the adjuster collars corrode and seize in coastal/salt-state cars. Photograph all four; a full set is $2,500–4,500, but Öhlins/authorized rebuild is roughly $250–400 per corner. Also budget front lower control arm bushings and rear links at 50–80k on the stiffer PE tune. 11) Brakes and regen: gold Brembo front calipers with slotted rotors cost real money ($1,200–2,000 for front pads and rotors), while the lightly used rear rotors rust, pit and seize their pads — very common on regen-heavy PHEVs, especially Midwest cars. Brake fluid is a strict 2-year/every-other-service item on this platform. 12) Tires and wheels: 4,800+ lb curb weight on 235/40R19 or 245/35R19 performance rubber means 15–25k-mile tire life and $1,300–1,800 a set; the forged PE wheels curb easily and bend on potholes. 13) Electronics and software: Sensus (through MY2022) and Google built-in (MY2023+) both suffe
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full dealer-level scan and software update to current calibration with all open campaigns closed; load-test and likely replace the 12V AGM (and support battery) if over 4 years or if the car has sat; brake fluid flush if not documented within 2 years; rear caliper/pad service or rotor replacement if regen rust has set in; coolant level/leak check across both engine and HV battery circuits; verified full Level 2 charge cycle; four-wheel alignment and corner-balance check of the Öhlins settings; cabin filter, wiper blades, and a pano-roof drain clean-out. If oil history is thin or the car lived on electricity, an immediate oil and filter change with an oil analysis sample.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Transaxle fluid and filter service if there is no record of one; engine oil at 5,000–7,500-mile intervals rather than the optimistic factory display; spark plugs if approaching 60k; front Brembo pads and slotted rotors depending on wear; Öhlins inspection with rebuild of any weeping or seized corner; front control arm and rear link bushings if clunks appear; a set of tires ($1,300–1,800) unless recently replaced; HV battery state-of-health recheck at annual service to trend degradation while the 8-year/100k hybrid warranty is still live; timing belt on any 2019–2020 example on age alone.
profiles.market_notes: The PE was a very low-volume halo trim (a few hundred US cars per year) and wagons command a clear premium over the S60 PE sedan, but depreciation from an ~$75–80k MSRP is brutal — good cars land in the high-$30k to mid-$40k band. The biggest price movers are remaining factory warranty (48-month/50k bumper-to-bumper; staying under 50k miles matters), documented Volvo dealer service history, and model year: 2022+ cars with 455 hp, 18.8 kWh and no supercharger are worth a premium over 2019–21 400 hp cars. Colors matter less than condition, though Thunder Grey/Onyx over the PE's gold-belt charcoal Nappa is the default and the rarer Bright Dusk or Crystal White cars draw more attention; low-mile, single-owner, non-salt-state examples with clean Carfax and no accident history are the ones that clear top money. Multiple owners, lease returns, thin records, or a rust-belt address should all pull the number down.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a 27k-mile example is a calendar-maintenance car: brake fluid (2-year), 12V AGM (4–6 year), coolant condition in both circuits, and tires/rubber that age out long before they wear out. Low-mileage PHEVs typically need rear brake de-rusting, an oil change on time-based schedule regardless of miles, and a software bring-up at the dealer; any 2019–2020 car should also be priced with a timing belt on the horizon.

The engine-bay photo shows the factory airbox, factory intake tube and no visible header or aftermarket piping, and the underbody photos show a factory-appearing catalyst and exhaust — so no hardware emissions exposure is visible. An ECU flash (current or removed) cannot be seen in a photo and has not been ruled out by a scan.
NHTSA 18V772000 covers 2013-model-year FA20 cars only. This is a 2016 build (VIN decode and invoice both read 2016/'16'), and an NHTSA query on 2026-09-22 returned zero open recalls for this vehicle.

NHTSA 21V587000 covers 2018-2019 low-pressure fuel pumps; this 2016 car is outside the campaign. Separately, the seller reports a 2018 warranty fuel-pump replacement under a service bulletin for a chirping noise — undocumented, and not the same campaign.

documentation.rationale: Identity and terms are strong: VIN present and matched to a dealer invoice, clean VA title stated, one-owner-from-new story, auction format and close time public, equipment itemised. What is missing is the rest: no Carfax attached to the tracker, no invoice for the June 2026 pads and rotors, no record of the 2018 warranty fuel pump, and nothing covering the decade of ownership before 2024. The seller's comment answers are unusually candid but they are still prose, not receipts.

condition.rationale: Positives first: the engine bay photographs clean and dry with factory intake hardware, the undertrays are present and undamaged, paint looks straight in the side profile with consistent gaps, and mileage is low for the year. Against that, the seller discloses chips, scratches, dings, upholstery wear and underbody corrosion, and the photos back the corrosion up — rust on the battery hold-down bracket and surrounding tray, rust on the rear suspension links, hardware and exhaust hangers, and mottled staining on the fuel tank shield. That reads as salt-exposure surface rust from the Virginia years rather than structural rot, but it needs a lift inspection. The original clutch at 58,800 miles with disclosed autocross and HPDE use is the other open condition item, and no compression, leakdown or oil-consumption data exists.

price_value.rationale: Comparable Cars & Bids results: a 2017 Limited with 46,900 miles sold at $16,400 and a 2016 Series.HyperBlue with 42,000 miles was bid to $17,039 without meeting reserve. At $3,500 with five bids the current number means nothing; the reserve is the real question. Marks come off only for the cosmetic wear and the salt-country underbody on a car that would be far more special as a rust-free West Coast example.

evidence.mission_note: This is a legitimate utility_capability candidate - body-on-frame, low range, roof rack and a fitted sleeping platform deliver camping capability the RX 350 simply does not have - but it is built well beyond the stated intent, and the brief explicitly says heavy off-road hardware (big lift, winch, armour) earns no premium and can signal hard use. In accelerated_bridge mode it is not a bridge car either: poor economy and a heavily modified 16-year-old truck are the opposite of a low-risk daily, so it only makes sense as a deliberate second-purpose vehicle bought at stock-equivalent money.
evidence.rationale: Evidence quality here is better than a typical Facebook private sale but still short of verified. The attached seller document is genuinely useful: a mileage-itemised log from 104,971 to 126,462 miles showing six oil changes, a full fluid and spark plug service at 105k, a timing-cover inspection with no coolant leak at 119k, a smog pass at 121,594 and OEM front brakes at 126,462 - plus a complete build list naming the installing shop. It is still the owner's own typed log rather than invoices, and it covers only the last 23,000 miles; the first 105,000 miles and 13 years have no record at all. The two expensive GX460 questions remain open: KDSS hydraulic condition is unaddressed (the Dr KDSS adapters confirm the system exists and was lift-corrected, nothing more), and secondary air injection rests on a self-reported smog pass from 6,400 miles ago with no scan. The build is the pricing problem: $22,500, already cut from $25,000 after eight weeks, against 2010 comps at $14,250 sold (142,900 mi), $16,995 asking (173,709 mi) and $9,800 sold (230,000 mi), and a 2012 Luxury at 118k that sold for $17,500 in Orange, CA. Roughly $5-7k of the ask is hardware the buyer's brief says is worth no premium, and the body-mount chop and viper cut are irreversible. On the positive side the mission fit is real - the rack and fitted sleeping platform match exactly the camping formats planned - and logistics are excellent at 75-80 miles from Carmel with easy PPI access. Nothing in the listing establishes a specific current fault, so there is no known-repair charge; the risk is concentrated in what a KDSS and underbody inspection would reveal and in overpaying for someone else's build.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller for the VIN and the Dirt Direct Offroad and 105k-service invoices, and ask to book an off-site PPI at a Bay Area Toyota/Lexus or 4x4 specialist with explicit KDSS lean measurement, a full readiness scan and underbody photos of the chopped body mounts - then negotiate from stock-equivalent comps, not from the $15k mod spend.

contradictions.detail: The dealer writes that 'we have loved experiencing this Cayman' over errands and canyon drives while also crediting a fastidious previous owner, yet no dealer-ownership dates or miles added are given and Carfax lists the car as a personal vehicle with 5 previous owners. Not incompatible, but the custody period immediately before sale is undefined.

critical_evidence.evidence: Nothing in the listing text, seller comments or attached photos refers to a borescope, cylinder-wall images or an engine inspection by a Porsche specialist. This is an M97 3.4 Cayman S, the exact engine for which the profile makes a scope mandatory; the absence of oil-consumption complaints is not evidence of clean bores.
No DME over-rev/range report is mentioned or shown. With five previous owners and self-described canyon use, range 3-6 data is exactly what would be needed.

Listing states water pump, thermostat and serpentine belt replaced April 2023, brakes April 2024, oil change March 2026, front tires/TPMS and front bump stops in 2026, and that service records accompany the car — but no invoices, scans or record summary are presented, and the AOS and coolant pipes are not mentioned at all.

documentation.rationale: Identity and terms are strong: full VIN, lot number, itemised option list, stated $0 dealer charges, clean California title claim and a Carfax snapshot showing 5 owners, 21 service records and no reported damage. Maintenance and condition evidence is the weak half: dated service claims (water pump/thermostat/belt 2023, brakes 2024, oil 2026) appear only as prose, with no invoice images, and the two pieces of evidence that matter most on an M97 S — a specialist borescope and a DME over-rev report — are entirely absent.

condition.rationale: Photos show a genuinely tidy car: deep Midnight Blue paint with good reflections, straight panels and gaps, unmarked 18" S wheels, red calipers on cross-drilled rotors, and a Natural Brown interior with only light seat and trim wear. The rear underbody image shows normal surface oxidation on cats and hardware with no rust-through, fresh coolant staining or crash repair in view. Against that: the seller discloses a hood paint chip, valence scratches and interior wear at the trunk trim, seatbelt and ignition, rear tire age is unstated, and clutch, AOS, coolant pipes and cylinder-wall condition are all unexamined here.

price_value.rationale: At $25,000 with six days and a live reserve, this clean 60k-mile California manual S sits below the recent BaT and private comps (2007 S 70k at $34,500; 2007 S 40k at $29,500; 2006 S 64k at $25,750) and will very likely run past Jason's $27,000 max price before the hammer, with a buyer fee on top. The profile prices good 2.7 manuals at $22-26k and says the S premium must be justified by the borescope — here the premium would be paid with no engine due diligence at all, which is the worst possible risk-adjusted trade.

mission_fit.rationale: As a future keeper a 987.1 Cayman S 6-speed is exactly the right kind of car — mid-engine, manual, Porsche, a car to hold. But the mission allows a higher price only for genuine superiority WITH documentation, and this car offers spec and presentation rather than engine evidence. It also conflicts with cash preservation while the 335i still needs replacing: it is not a bridge car, and buying it does not solve the near-term problem.

logistics.rationale: Hawthorne is roughly a 330-mile drive from Carmel — a one-day inspection trip and an enjoyable drive home. The dealer explicitly invites in-person inspection and PPI, the car is California-registered from new so smog transfer should be routine, and $0 additional dealer charges are stated. The only pressure is the 6-day auction clock, which means a specialist borescope appointment must be booked now, not after.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Midnight Blue Metallic over Natural Brown with the manual transaxle, Preferred Package Plus, bi-xenon and S wheels is close to the ideal 987 specification, and the photos confirm the combination works. Coupe, mid-engine, three pedals — this is squarely the enthusiast brief, not a pragmatic bridge.

ppi_focus: Borescope all six cylinders with retained photographs, with particular attention to cylinders 4-6 for vertical scoring and to the crosshatch condition.
DME over-rev and fault memory download, interpreted alongside a leakdown/compression test — never instead of the scope.
AOS function check (vacuum test) and inspection for oil mist in the intake tract and smoke on a cold start.
Cooling system: pressure test, inspect the 2023 water pump work, check the plastic coolant pipes and the radiators/condensers for debris and coastal corrosion.
Clutch engagement point, dual-mass flywheel rattle at idle, and transaxle shift quality across all six gears including 2nd cold.
Rear main seal / IMS area: inspect the bellhousing weep hole and record any oil residue; check for metallic debris in the oil filter media.
Suspension: rear control-arm and sway-bar bushings, front lower-arm bushings, shock condition, and confirm the new bump stops/dust covers are properly installed.
Rear tire date codes and any front/rear wear mismatch; verify TPMS function on all four corners.
Paint-depth readings on every panel to test the no-reported-accident Carfax, plus a lift inspection of the floorpan, jack points and front valence damage.
Confirm PCM, Bose, heated seats, spoiler deployment and climate control all operate.
what_would_change_verdict: A dated independent Porsche-specialist borescope with clean photos of cylinders 4-6, plus a clean DME over-rev report, would transform this from a gamble into a legitimate keeper candidate.
Invoice photographs for the 2023 cooling work, plus documented AOS and coolant-pipe service, would move documentation and condition materially upward.
A hammer price that stays inside the stated max price with fees included — unlikely given comps at $29,500-$34,500 — would fix the price-discipline problem.
Any borescope finding of scoring in 4-6, oil-consumption evidence, or a refusal to permit the scope before close should end interest immediately.
Evidence of a recent clutch/flywheel replacement with a receipt would remove one of the larger open 12-month costs.
evidence.mission_note: As a future keeper the specification is close to ideal — a manual 987.1 Cayman S in Midnight Blue over Natural Brown is a car to hold, not a bridge — but it does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem the 335i is creating and it commits cash at a moment when cash preservation matters. It is only defensible if the borescope and over-rev report come back clean AND the hammer stays disciplined; without the scope it is not buyable at any price under this profile.
evidence.rationale: The decisive fact is what is not here: this is an M97 3.4 Cayman S and the listing contains no borescope, no cylinder photographs and no DME over-rev report, which the model profile treats as a hard requirement — seller silence on oil use is not evidence of clean bores. Everything else is encouraging: a lifelong California car, a Carfax snapshot with no reported damage, 5 owners and 21 service entries, and a narrative of real maintenance (water pump, thermostat and serpentine belt April 2023, brakes April 2024, oil March 2026, front tires, TPMS and front bump stops in 2026), though all of it appears as prose rather than as invoice images. The photographs support the condition story — deep Midnight Blue paint, straight panels, unmarked S wheels, a lightly worn Natural Brown interior and a rear underbody with only normal surface oxidation and no rust-through — while the seller himself discloses a hood chip, valence scratches and interior wear at the trunk trim, seatbelt and ignition. Rear tire age is unstated even though the fronts were replaced this year, so a matching rear pair should be budgeted. Logistics are as good as they get: Hawthorne is a day trip from Carmel, the dealer explicitly invites PPI and extra photos, and there are no additional dealer charges. The pricing is the second problem: at $25,000 with six days, an undisclosed reserve and comps at $25,750-$34,500 for similar-mileage S cars, the realistic hammer band is $29,000-$36,000 before the buyer fee, well past the max price in the state block. The catch-up bill is also ordinary-but-real for an 18-year-old 987: fluids, AOS if unknown, cooling inspection, rear tires, with clutch and coolant pipes lurking in the next twelve months. Net: an attractive, honestly presented car that cannot be bid on until the engine is scoped, and probably cannot be bought within budget even then.
evidence.next_action: Contact analog_garage today and book an independent Porsche-specialist borescope of all six cylinders plus a DME over-rev download in Hawthorne before the 24 September 12:47 Pacific close; do not place a bid until those photos and that report are in hand.

evidence.rationale: Hard gate unmet: there is no borescope on this 3.4 M97, and the original owner states in the comments that he never had one done, resting instead on no smoke and no oil consumption — precisely the symptom-based reassurance that counts as zero evidence here. Everything else about the car is better than average. The VIN-matched Autel DME scan is a genuinely good result (Ranges 4-6 all zero, one Range-3 stamp roughly 877 operating hours ago out of 1,827 total), the seller volunteered the 2011 accident that Carfax does not show and published the repair order, and three independent-shop invoices corroborate the odometer chain from 63,018 to 63,630. But those same invoices show what is absent: no water pump, no AOS, no coolant pipes, no clutch, nothing before 2024 despite the claim of records from new. They also show a cylinder 1 and 3 misfire diagnosed on 09 May 2026, four months before the auction, fixed with a camshaft solenoid, sensor, six coils and plugs, with no document proving it stayed fixed — and that sits uncomfortably beside a seller who writes that no work was needed. Comps put good 987.1 S manuals between $23,250 and $29,500, so the current $5,105 is an opening bid and nothing more. Logistics are excellent — Modesto is a short drive, the smog is fresh, the seller is responsive — which is exactly why the borescope should be booked rather than the risk accepted.

documentation.rationale: Identity and terms are strong: full VIN, factory option-code build list (PASM, Sport Chrono Plus, P78 sport seats, XCZ sport shifter, Bose, PCM 2.1, Bi-Xenon), Carfax with owner count and no reported damage, a documented prior BaT sale of the same VIN in Feb 2019 for $23,987, clean AZ title in the seller's name, and a named cooperative private seller. Maintenance-and-condition evidence is the weak half: the 2018 clutch and 2019 $8k cooling service are described in prose with records said to convey, but no invoice, no scan, no borescope report and no DME over-rev printout were available to review, and the 2020-2025 window is documented only by a single oil change. For the one engine risk that defines this model, documentation is empty.

condition.rationale: Presentation is good for 19 years and 70k miles: straight panels with even gaps, unmarked 18" Cayman S wheels, red calipers with cross-drilled rotors, and an exceptionally clean terracotta cabin with no bolster wear or dash cracking visible. The single underbody photo shows a dry, undamaged rear subframe and suspension with only surface grime and light whitish staining, no rot or fresh fluid. Against that, the seller discloses front bumper discoloration and clear-coat failure plus other body blemishes, and states the front strut bump stops are due. The determinative items — cylinder-wall condition on an M97 3.4, AOS, coolant pipes, tire date codes, bushings — are all unexamined, and unknowns on this engine pull hard.

price_value.rationale: Retail asks for 987.1 Cayman S manuals run $35-45k for 24-51k-mile cars, but recent auction reality is softer: 28k-mile S at $27,500 and a 103k-mile S at $23,250 on Cars & Bids, and a 21k-mile base 987.2 at $29,500 on BaT. A 70k-mile, six-owner S with a cosmetic bumper defect, all-season tires of unknown age and no bore evidence should land in the mid-to-high $20s, which sits at the top of the buyer's stated max_price and leaves little room for the engine-verification and catch-up spend a keeper Cayman S demands. The $3,000 current bid on day one carries no information. Excellent spec supports value; the missing borescope caps it.

mission_fit.rationale: As a future keeper this is the right shape of car: manual, mid-engine, PASM, Sport Chrono Plus, sport seats, single long-term owner for the last 7.5 years, and Porsche parts availability. But the profile is explicit that the 3.4 S is bought only with unusually strong engine due diligence, and this listing supplies none, on a 7-day auction clock. It also does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem — it is a discretionary keeper purchase that consumes the cash reserve while the 335i's coolant and suspension issues remain, and a Cayman S is a poor daily bridge. Attractive only as a keeper, and in direct tension with cash preservation.

logistics.rationale: Centerbrook, CT is a coast-to-coast trip — a cost and a scheduling item, and Jason will fly out and drive a good car home, which suits a sorted Cayman. The real logistics friction is the auction clock: a Porsche-specialist borescope, leakdown and DME pull in Connecticut must be booked and completed before bidding ends Sep 14, and nothing in the listing establishes that inspection access is available. BaT shipping is offered. California registration adds a step: the GMG exhaust's catalytic configuration is unstated, though the original exhaust conveying with the car is a workable path to a visual-inspection pass.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Close to the ideal 987.1 S order sheet: six-speed manual with sport shifter, PASM, Sport Chrono Package Plus, heated sport seats in full Special Leather Terracotta with matching dash and carpets, Bi-Xenons, Bose, thicker leather wheel. Arctic Silver over terracotta is a genuinely rare and warm combination that photographs beautifully and is far more special than a black-interior car. The GMG exhaust suits the character and is reversible with the included factory system. This is a car worth wanting.

ppi_focus: Specialist borescope of all six cylinders with retained photographs, prioritizing 4-6 for scoring and any evidence of scuffing on the thrust side (this is the go/no-go item).
Leakdown and compression on all cylinders, interpreted alongside the borescope images, never instead of them.
DME over-rev report and full fault-memory readout via PIWIS, including any stored misfire or over-temperature events.
Cooling system pressure test with attention to the plastic coolant pipes, radiators/condensers and the reservoir replaced in 2019.
AOS function test (crankcase vacuum measurement) and inspection for oil in the intake tract and smoke at cold start.
Clutch engagement point and drive quality versus the claimed May 2018 replacement; check for judder and rear main seal seepage at the bellhousing.
Front suspension: bump stops the seller flagged, plus strut condition, control-arm and sway-bar bushings, and steering-rack play.
Paint depth readings on all panels and inspection of the front bumper defect for prior repair, plus bumper mounts and radiator-area debris.
Brake rotor cross-drill crack inspection, pad life, and brake-fluid moisture content.
Rear subframe and underbody inspection for the whitish residue visible in photos — confirm it is road film rather than corrosion or a dried fluid trail.
what_would_change_verdict: A dated Porsche-specialist borescope with clear photos of cylinders 4-6 showing no scoring, plus leakdown figures and a clean DME over-rev report, would move this from speculative to a credible keeper.
Posted invoices for an AOS replacement and coolant-pipe inspection, plus documentation of any 2020-2025 service, would lift the documentation and condition ratings materially.
Confirmation that a specialist inspection can actually be completed in Connecticut before the September 14 close — without it, this is an unverifiable M97 bought on prose.

A hammer price near the Cars & Bids reality (low-to-mid $20s) rather than the retail asks would create room for the verification and catch-up spend; a hammer in the $30s makes it uncompetitive against a proven 2.7 manual.
Any borescope showing scoring, an over-rev report with hits in ranges 4-6, or evidence of undisclosed track use would end it outright.
evidence.mission_note: As a future_keeper this is the right kind of car — a rare-spec, long-owned, manual 987.1 Cayman S with the clutch and cooling work claimed done — but the profile's hard gate is a specialist borescope, and this listing supplies zero engine-internals evidence on a 7-day clock. It also does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem: it is a discretionary keeper that would absorb the cash reserve while the 335i still needs replacing, so it only makes sense if the borescope comes back clean and the hammer stays well under the top of budget.
evidence.rationale: This is an attractive keeper candidate that fails the model's one non-negotiable test as presented. Identity and terms are unusually well documented — VIN, a factory option-code build list confirming PASM, Sport Chrono Plus, P78 sport seats, Bose and the sport shifter, a clean Carfax with six prior owners, a clean AZ title in the seller's name, and a verifiable prior BaT sale of this exact VIN for $23,987 in February 2019 — but the maintenance-and-condition half is prose only. The May 2018 clutch/flywheel and the April 2019 ~$8,000 water pump, thermostat, coolant reservoir and belt service are exactly the right items, yet they are seven years old with only ~8k miles added since, no invoice was reviewable here, and a commenter's question about what has been done since 2020 beyond a November 2025 oil change sits unanswered. Most importantly, this is the M97 3.4 at 70k miles with no borescope, no leakdown and no DME over-rev report, on a car whose owner explicitly brought it east for track time; the profile treats specialist cylinder imaging of 4-6 as a hard requirement and seller assurances of good health are not evidence. Photos support genuinely good condition — straight panels, even gaps, unmarked 18" wheels, a dry undamaged rear subframe, and a terracotta cabin with no visible wear — while the seller honestly discloses front bumper clear-coat failure, other blemishes, and front strut bump stops due, which are the known-work items. Auction comps say a 70k-mile six-owner S without bore evidence belongs in the mid-$20s, not at the $35-45k retail asks, which puts a realistic hammer right at the top of the buyer's price ceiling before any verification or catch-up spend. Spec and emotional fit are close to ideal and the seller is cooperative, so the path forward is inspection access, not rejection. Without a borescope completed before September 14, this is an unverified M97 bought on faith.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller today to arrange a pre-auction Porsche-specialist appointment in the Centerbrook, CT area for a six-cylinder borescope with retained photos of cylinders 4-6, a leakdown test and a PIWIS over-rev/fault pull, and ask him to post the 2018 clutch and 2019 cooling invoices plus tire date codes in the comments; do not bid until those images exist.

price_value.rationale: No reserve with a $1,750 opening bid and seven days to run; the only comp given is a 2012 Sport with 57k miles at $15,500 (Cars & Bids, April 2026), and this car sold for $11,000 in April 2024 with 13k fewer miles, before the tune/intake/exhaust were a resale question and before the accident-free premium mattered. ppi_focus: Cooling system: pressure-test the expansion tank and hoses cold, verify electric water pump operation and coolant temperature control under load, and check pump/thermostat part date stamps
Oil leaks: inspect oil-filter-housing gasket, valve-cover gasket and oil-pan gasket on a lift after degrease, and check the alternator bracket area for oil contamination
Full fault-code scan of all modules with attention to the brake module (the disclosed service brake light) and DME adaptations reflecting the tune
Underside corrosion survey: rear subframe mounting points, trailing-arm bushings, brake and fuel lines, exhaust hangers, and whether fasteners are seizing
Front and right-front structure: check radiator support, inner fender, headlight mounts and bumper reinforcement for the April 2019 damage, plus paint depth readings on all panels
Clutch and manual gearbox: engagement point, pedal feel, no shudder, verify July 2024 work quality and check for rear-main or gearbox seal seepage
Suspension: condition of the Bilstein/Eibach setup, front control-arm bushings and rear shock mounts, plus ride height and any bind from the aftermarket springs
Valvetronic/VANOS operation and cold-start noise on the N52; verify no lifter tick or eccentric shaft sensor codes
Tire date codes, tread depth, and confirmation all four match
Verify open recall status at a BMW dealer, especially the PCV heater and airbag inflator campaigns
what_would_change_verdict: Receipts showing the electric water pump, thermostat and expansion tank replaced within the last few years would remove the largest unknown and move this up materially.

A clean independent PPI on a lift confirming no oil-filter-housing or pan leaks, sound structure at the right front, and surface-only underside rust would justify bidding to the low end of the expected range.
The seller including the stock DME file and factory intake — making a return to CARB-legal configuration a same-day job — would resolve the California registration risk and the resale drag.
A scan proving the brake lamp is a simple wear sensor, with a quote to fix, would convert an open fault into a $200 line item.
If no PPI can be arranged before the 9/13 close, or if the scan shows cooling/oil-leak codes or structural repair at the right front, walk away regardless of price.
evidence.mission_note: This is the right shape of car for the enthusiast-bridge mission — manual, naturally aspirated N52, rear-drive, cheap to exit — and at no reserve it should land inside the $10-13k target. But the tune plus intake, an undiagnosed brake warning light, an undocumented cooling system and a salted Midwest underside make it a project-adjacent bridge rather than a turn-key one, and in accelerated_bridge mode that matters.
evidence.rationale: The result is a conditional yes only with a lift-based PPI and cooling documentation before the 9/13 close. The mechanicals that usually kill these cars have partly been addressed and dated: clutch and hydraulics July 2024, coils and plugs September 2024, brakes 2025, rear shock mounts under prior ownership — and the seller specifically bought an N52 to avoid turbo complexity, the same logic driving Jason away from the 335i. Against that, the listing itself discloses an undiagnosed service brake lamp that is 'often on,' a Carfax front/right-front damage entry from April 2019 with no repair documentation plus bumper-cover paintwork, a torn driver's seat bolster, and 'rust visible on underside components' that the underside photo confirms as heavy surface corrosion on the rear suspension hardware. The two model-critical files — electric water pump/thermostat/expansion tank history and oil-filter-housing/valve-cover/pan leak status — are entirely absent, and a pre-sale oil change makes visual leak assessment harder, so both must be treated as unknown and budgeted. The aftermarket ECU tune and intake break the profile's stock-powertrain requirement, create a California smog and registration step, and will cost money on resale in the 6-24 month window the mission cares about. Provenance is at least honest and traceable: same car, $11,000 on BaT in April 2024, 13k miles ago. At no reserve with $1,750 bid and a week to run, the price should stay in range, but the all-in should be figured with roughly $1,100-$3,200 of known work plus transport from Quincy, IL on top of the hammer.
evidence.next_action: Before bidding, book an independent BMW specialist near Quincy, IL for a lift PPI plus full module scan this week, and ask the seller in the comments for cooling-system receipts and confirmation that a stock DME file and factory intake come with the car.

documentation.rationale: Real strengths: published VIN, Carfax with 8 service and 44 detailed records, owner's manuals, a photographed records folder, build-bench photos of the forged rotating assembly, and a named tuning shop. But every substantive claim about the build, the clutch, the LSD and the A/C rebuild is 'reportedly/said to be' in listing prose; no invoices, dyno sheet, machine-shop paperwork, compression numbers or 2008 accident repair documentation are reproduced. Long single ownership through the build helps, but for a car whose value rests entirely on build quality, the verifiable layer is thin.

condition.rationale: Presentation is genuinely strong: straight silver panels with even reflections, tidy shutlines, intact sport seat bolsters, an uncracked dash top, and an engine bay that looks assembled with care. Recent hardware is dated and plausible — 2026 brake overhaul (master, calipers, rotors, pads), 2026 tires, 2024 subframe/control arms/wheel bearings, 2024 driveshaft center bearing and CV boots. The single underbody photo is clean and dry. What pulls it down is what is not shown: no shock tower, trunk battery corner or floor photos on a Canadian-market car, no health data on a 2022 built engine (leakdown, coolant temps, oil pressure log), and a documented front-end collision whose inner structure has never been photographed.

price_value.rationale: At the captured $3,600 opening bid it looks cheap, but this is a reserve auction with 258 watchers and a build story; realistic hammer is well into the mid-to-high teens plus 5% buyer fee, which lands above Jason's $15k all-in bridge target and near his ideal band ceiling. Against the peer 1987 325is at $11,000, this is a four-cylinder 318is with a Carfax moderate accident, repainted front clip, a bespoke standalone-managed engine and non-CARB hardware — exactly the profile that the documentation-driven E30 market discounts on resale. You would be paying enthusiast-build money for an asset whose next buyer pool is narrow.

mission_fit.rationale: It clears the manual requirement and it is local and inspectable, but the mission asks for a reliable, easy-to-resell, sub-$15k-all-in bridge with low ownership friction. A 10.5:1 forged M42 on ITBs and a Haltech tune, with a cat-delete pipe and CARB-questionable hardware in a state where Jason must smog it every two years, is the opposite of low friction — and his mechanic does VW/Toyota, not standalone tuning. Resale in 6-24 months depends on finding another E30 build buyer rather than the broad market.

logistics.rationale: San Mateo is roughly 85 miles from Carmel — a same-day drive for a PPI and a drive home. Seller is a private party, publicly responsive, offering additional photos, videos and records, plus a new catalytic converter, the stock airboxes and a current passing California smog certificate to a California buyer. California title in his name, no transport needed. The only logistics friction is the auction clock (closes 2026-09-11) which compresses PPI scheduling.

It falls short of the profile's ideal on two counts: it is a 318is four rather than the M20 325is six the buyer's brief describes, and it is a heavily modified car rather than a preserved, documented original — the character is the builder's, not the factory's.

Drivetrain: 325is LSD lock-up test (one-wheel spin), diff and output seal leaks, driveshaft center bearing vibration at 45-60 mph, clutch engagement and any throwout squeal.
Suspension and steering after the E36 M3 rack conversion: alignment printout, bump steer, poly bushing NVH, ball joints, tie rods and Bilstein damper condition.
Electrical: instrument cluster odometer/OBC operation on the km cluster, A/C output temperature after the claimed rebuild, sunroof operation, LED headlight beam pattern legality.
Emissions dry-run: confirm the car can be presented smog-legal with the supplied cat and stock intake, ideally by taking it to a smog shop as part of the PPI.
what_would_change_verdict: Full build invoices plus a clean leakdown and a Haltech datalog showing normal coolant temps and AFR, combined with lift photos or a specialist PPI confirming no structural damage from the 2008 front hit and no rust — that would move it from a speculative build to a documented one.
A BAR referee certificate (or a smog certificate obtained in the exact configuration the car will be delivered in) that makes California registration a non-issue rather than an open liability.
A hammer price that keeps all-in under about $13,000 including fee and the compliance work — at that number the risk is priced in and it becomes a defensible fun bridge.
Bidding past roughly $16,000 all-in, or a PPI finding poor front-end repair, coolant-temp problems on the built motor, or shock-tower/subframe corrosion — any of those should end it.
Seller declining or slow-walking a pre-auction PPI at an independent Bay Area BMW specialist would make this a pass on principle.
evidence.mission_note: As an enthusiast bridge this is charismatic and geographically ideal but mission-adverse: a forged, standalone-tuned, cat-deleted 318is is a specialist toy that Jason's VW/Toyota mechanic cannot support, that carries an unresolved California emissions question, and that resells to a narrow build-buyer audience rather than quickly. It is not a pragmatic bridge either — the whole point of the bridge is dependable, cheap, easy-to-exit, and this car is none of those three despite looking the part.
evidence.rationale: This is a well-presented, heavily engineered E30 that fails the brief for structural reasons rather than cosmetic ones. The verifiable evidence is decent for a private BaT car — published VIN, Carfax with 8 service and 44 detailed records, build-bench photos, a named tuner, nine years of single ownership, and dated recent work (2026 brakes and tires, 2024 subframe, control arms, wheel bearings, driveshaft center bearing, CV boots) — but the entire value proposition, the 2022 forged 2.0L M42 with Haltech and ITBs, is supported only by seller prose: no invoices, no leakdown, no logs, no machine-shop paperwork. Carfax records an October 2008 moderate front-damage accident and a 2009 damage claim, the hood and front fenders are repainted, and no inner-structure photos or repair documentation exist. The car was a California Gross Polluter in 2021 and currently runs a catalyst-delete pipe with hardware the listing itself admits may not be CARB-certified, which sits in direct tension with the seller's promise of a passing smog certificate. It is a Canadian-market import with no shock-tower, trunk-corner or floor photos, so rust is unknown, not absent. Logistics are excellent — San Mateo, cooperative seller, easy PPI — and the emotional pull is real, but a reserve auction with 258 watchers points to a mid-to-high-teens hammer plus fee, above the sub-$15k all-in bridge target, for an asset that is harder to resell and harder to service than the GTI, F56 or 128i alternatives. Buy only on a clean specialist PPI, full build receipts, and a price that stays cheap.
evidence.next_action: Before bidding, book a pre-auction PPI at an independent Bay Area BMW/standalone-EFI specialist (leakdown, cooling pressure test, Haltech datalog, lift inspection of the repaired front clip and shock towers) and simultaneously ask the seller in the comments for the engine build invoices and the configuration of the December 2024 smog certificate.

documentation.rationale: What exists is a Carfax summary (12 service entries, 3 owners, a 2016 left-front damage entry) plus seller prose. There is no invoice folder, no Porsche or independent service file, no water-pump or brake-fluid record, no clutch/DMF history, no DME over-rev report, no borescope, and no repair documentation for the disclosed damage. Carfax line items are third-hand references, not receipts, and the seller has left the highest-value documentation requests in the comments unanswered.

condition.rationale: Presentation is genuinely good: photos show straight dark blue paint after a paint correction and ceramic coating, clean pebble-gray leather with no obvious bolster wear, tidy 20" wheels, and a dry-looking rear underbody with no rust. Positives on record: headlights replaced 2024 (a $2k+ item pre-paid), plugs and serpentine belt 2022, fresh oil. Against that, at 78k miles and 12 years the water pump, brake fluid, coolant, AGM battery, clutch/DMF and PASM/damper condition are all undocumented, the tires are non-N-spec Nittos of unknown age, the left-front was damaged in 2016 with no repair record, and the single most catastrophic risk on this engine (bore scoring) has no borescope or consumption evidence at all.

price_value.rationale: At the current $17,500 no-reserve bid this is well under market for a 981 manual, which is the configuration the market pays a premium for. Realistically it will run higher; a base 2.7 with 78k miles, a Carfax damage entry and undocumented aftermarket exhaust should trade below a clean documented car, so value stays good up to roughly $23k hammer (~$24.2k with BaT fee) and evaporates as it approaches the mid-$20s where documented cars and Boxster S examples appear. Add ~$1,500 transport and $1,600-$2,600 of known tire work and the all-in crowds Jason's $27,000 max quickly.

mission_fit.rationale: As a future keeper the 981 manual is exactly right — last NA mid-engine Porsche roadster, no IMS, superb on Highway 1 and the Laureles Grade, and a manual, which the buyer requires. But the keeper case rests on documentation and originality, and this car is the undocumented, damage-reported, modified-exhaust version of the recipe. It is also the cash-heavier path at a moment when the strategy calls for preserving cash against the 335i's exit; it does not solve the bridge problem, it is a discretionary keeper purchase.

logistics.rationale: North Royalton, Ohio is a fly-out-and-drive-home car, which is a cost item and fine in principle — but the auction ends 2026-09-09, roughly three days out, which is a tight window to book a Cleveland-area Porsche specialist for a borescope, DME pull and cooling pressure test, and the dealer has not responded to simpler requests. The larger logistics issue is California: an out-of-state 2014 with unidentified aftermarket exhaust must pass a smog inspection with visual catalyst verification, and nobody has confirmed the cats are intact.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Dark Blue Metallic over Pebble/Agate Gray with a blue top, Sport seats, SportDesign wheel, bi-xenon PDLS and 20" Carrera S wheels is a genuinely handsome, non-default spec, and a manual open-top flat-six in Carmel is close to ideal. Points off because it is the 2.7 base without Sport Chrono or PSE, and the fake-S dual central exhaust is exactly the kind of 'appear to be something it isn't' modification that grates on an originality-minded owner and shaves resale.

evidence.mission_note: As a future_keeper this is the right car in the wrong condition of evidence: a genuine 981 manual in an attractive spec, but with a damage entry, undocumented aftermarket exhaust, and none of the model-critical engine or top evidence supplied. It does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem — a two-seat convertible will not replace the 335i's daily role — so it is a discretionary keeper buy that competes directly with the cash needed for the bridge car.
evidence.rationale: Verdict driver: the evidence file is thin on exactly the items that decide whether a 78k-mile 9A1 is a bargain or a $20,000 mistake. No borescope, no DME over-rev report (and the DME itself was replaced in 2021, per Carfax, which may have truncated that history), no water-pump or brake-fluid record, and no full top-cycle video despite a bidder asking for one on September 4. Carfax does establish a February 2016 'minor damage' event to the left and left-front, and no repair documentation is offered — while a fresh paint correction and ceramic coating have just been applied over the area. The 'aftermarket exhaust components' are the second material issue: the rear photo shows S-style dual central outlets on a base 2.7 and the underside photo shows a non-factory rear section, but two commenters have asked whether cats or headers are involved and the seller has answered neither, which is a live California smog-and-registration question, not a cosmetic quibble. On the positive side the car photographs well — straight dark blue panels, clean Pebble Gray leather with no visible bolster wear, a dry rust-free rear underbody — and it carries real pre-paid value in the March 2024 headlight replacement plus 2022 plugs and serpentine belt. The tires are non-N-spec Nittos of unstated age, so budget a set plus alignment as known work, on top of $3,200-$5,800 of first-year catch-up for cooling, fluids, battery and top service. At $17,500 no reserve it is cheap; at the $22k-$28k range this configuration usually reaches, the discount for the damage entry and the fake-S exhaust disappears and the buyer is paying near-documented-car money for an undocumented car. Everything hinges on getting a specialist onto it in the three days remaining.
evidence.next_action: Today, book a Porsche specialist near North Royalton, OH for a pre-close PPI with borescope of all six cylinders, DME over-rev/PIWIS pull, cooling pressure test, lift photos confirming both catalytic converters, and three full top cycles — and post the exhaust and DME questions publicly in the BaT comments so a non-answer is on the record before bidding.

evidence.rationale: The result is driven by evidence that is almost entirely seller prose. The two items that set GX470 value — timing-belt documentation and rear-suspension status — are both absent: a bidder asked about the belt on Aug 31 and the seller simply never answered, and the AVS/height control appears only as an equipment line. Worse, two separate commenters read the underside photos as undercoating over bubbling corrosion on a truck the listing itself says was last owned in Pennsylvania, and the dealer's rebuttal is three sentences with no close-up photos posted. Frame rust is a hard reject on this profile, and unknown here is not good. The listing does disclose real defects honestly — cracked dash (a $1,700-2,500 job by the comment thread's own estimate) and touched-up roof and bumper covers — and the truck presents well in the photos: straight, stock, tidy engine bay, intact undershields. documentation.rationale: Identity and terms are strong: full VIN, lot number, itemised option list, stated $0 dealer charges, clean California title claim and a Carfax snapshot showing 5 owners, 21 service records and no reported damage. condition.rationale: Photos show a genuinely tidy car: deep Midnight Blue paint with good reflections, straight panels and gaps, unmarked 18" S wheels, red calipers on cross-drilled rotors, and a Natural Brown interior with only light seat and trim wear. price_value.rationale: At $25,000 with six days and a live reserve, this clean 60k-mile California manual S sits below the recent BaT and private comps (2007 S 70k at $34,500; 2007 S 40k at $29,500; 2006 S 64k at $25,750) and will very likely run past Jason's $27,000 max price before the hammer, with a buyer fee on top.
